name: Lena Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a field supervisor at Brook Lane Growers. We grow broccoli, leeks and salad onions for two of the big supermarkets, about four hundred hectares. In summer I run a crew of around forty pickers, most from abroad, and my day starts at five with the harvest plan and ends when the last lorry leaves the cold store. The supermarket can change an order at eleven at night and we just have to find a way.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part and the worst part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best part is the crew. When it's going well, the rigs are moving, everyone's laughing, and we fill the order early, it's honestly great. Worst part is the buyers. They reject a whole load because the broccoli heads are two centimetres too small, and then I'm the one telling forty people there's no overtime this week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI at work at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I use a translation app on my phone with some of the crew, and I've asked a chatbot to help me write a rota once or twice. I wouldn't trust it with anything important yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So basically what we've got now, plus a bit. Fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the real problem in farming was never technology, it's the supermarkets squeezing growers. I'd post something like that, actually, I do sometimes. Nobody's job was going to be saved or lost by a better chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, it'd be a relief for the crew more than for me. A lot of them send money home and a picking robot would hit them before it hit me. I'd still be stuck fighting buyers over centimetres, which is the bit that really wears me down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing my job, and probably use the translation and rota tools a bit more since they'd be proven by then. I'd keep paying into my savings and maybe overpay on my flat a little. I'd also keep pushing the boss to sign up with the growers' union so we've got someone talking to the supermarkets for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit flat, maybe, because the things I'd actually like changed wouldn't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you most like changed, if it isn't the technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair prices and fair contracts. If the supermarket wants perfect broccoli, it should pay for the ones that aren't perfect too. Half a field gets ploughed back in some years and nobody outside the farm ever sees it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your crew would you be thinking about here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta, mostly. She's been coming every season for six years and she's faster than any of us on the rig. She's saving for a house back home and she counts every hour.

S0.say: She'd say the real problem in farming was never technology but supermarkets squeezing growers. She'd post that a better chatbot was never going to save or lose anyone's job.
S0.think: She's relieved mostly for her seasonal pickers, who would be hit before she was. She'd still be stuck arguing with supermarket buyers, which is the part of the job that wears her down.
S0.do: Carries on as field supervisor and uses translation and rota tools a little more once proven. Keeps saving, overpays a little on her flat and keeps pressing her boss to join the growers' union.
S0.feel: Calm but a bit flat, because the things she really wants changed, prices and contracts, stay the same.
S0.quote: Half a field gets ploughed back in some years and nobody outside the farm ever sees it.
S0.fieldNote: Lena turns the plateau question straight into a complaint about supermarket power, which is where her anger lives. She thinks first of her crew, especially Marta, before herself. Her own position is comfortable: savings, a flat, and plenty of similar jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: OK, this one feels real. I can already picture who'd go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the pickers need a proper plan before the robots come in, training, notice and money. I'd say it at work, and I'd sign whatever petition the union put out. Growers get grants for machines, so workers should get grants for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job would change rather than vanish. I'd go from running forty people to running ten people and six robot harvesters, and I'd be fine. That's what makes me uncomfortable, honestly, that I'd be fine and Marta wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a couple of farms near us had the harvesters working properly, then ask to be trained on them, probably in the second year. I'd push hard in the union for notice periods for seasonal crews. And I'd help the crew with their CVs and translations, which I'd actually use the AI for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit guilty. Guilty is the main word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until other farms had the harvesters working. Why not be first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first ones always break. I watched the farm up the road buy an expensive weeding robot that got stuck in wet clay for a whole month. I'll learn it once it works, not while it's still a science project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marta if her season got cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the truth early, before she books her flight. And I'd write her the best reference I've ever written. That's not much, I know that.

S1.say: She'd say seasonal pickers need a proper plan, with training, notice and money, before robots arrive. If growers get grants for machines, workers should get grants for retraining.
S1.think: She expects her own job to change rather than disappear, from running forty people to running ten people and some robot harvesters. What troubles her is that she'd be fine and her crew wouldn't.
S1.do: Waits until nearby farms have harvesters working well, then asks to be trained on them in about the second year. Pushes the union for notice periods for seasonal crews and uses AI to help pickers with CVs and translations.
S1.feel: Uneasy and above all guilty that she'd come out ahead of her crew.
S1.quote: That's what makes me uncomfortable, honestly, that I'd be fine and Marta wouldn't.
S1.fieldNote: The steady pattern shows clearly: Lena will adopt the harvesters, but only after a neighbour proves them, as with the weeding robot stuck in clay. Her guilt is the strongest feeling in this picture. She'd turn AI tools towards helping the crew leave well, not towards her own advancement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028. That's three more harvests. I don't think the farm could even get the machines that fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency rules, like they did in the pandemic: income support for everyone it hits, and no supermarket gets to use it as an excuse to cut prices again. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen. I'd go to the protests too, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think everyone at Brook Lane is out, me included, within a year of it landing. If a robot can pick, pack, plan and argue with buyers, they don't need a supervisor. I've got savings and a flat, so I'm not on the street, but I wouldn't know what I'm for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd stop overpaying the flat and keep the cash where I can get it. I'd get the crew organised to demand proper pay-offs, and I'd help the foreign workers with visas and getting home safely. Then I honestly don't know, I'd probably look into community food projects, because people would still need to eat and someone needs to run things locally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. And a bit lost, like the floor's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years' warning change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means there's no time to do things in the proper order. With a few years you'd train, then switch, then help people. In two years it'd all be at once, and the people without savings would just drop through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still have savings and a flat. Does that make it better or worse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. Better because I can eat and sleep. Worse because I'd feel like I should be doing something huge with that safety, and I wouldn't know what.

S2.say: She'd call for emergency rules like in the pandemic: income support for everyone hit, and no letting supermarkets use it to cut prices again. She'd say it to anyone and probably join protests.
S2.think: She thinks the whole farm, herself included, would be out within a year, because a machine that can pick, pack, plan and deal with buyers needs no supervisor. Her savings and flat keep her safe, but she wouldn't know what she's for.
S2.do: Stops overpaying her flat to keep cash to hand, organises the crew to demand proper pay-offs and helps foreign workers with visas and getting home. Then looks into running local community food projects.
S2.feel: Alarmed and lost, as if the floor had gone.
S2.quote: I've got savings and a flat, so I'm not on the street, but I wouldn't know what I'm for.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture removes the thing Lena relies on, time to wait for proof, and she freezes on her own future while moving fast for others. Her cushion makes her physically safe but raises a question of purpose. Supermarkets stay the villain even here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is more like it. Still fast, but you'd at least see it coming across the field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when the union and the government have to plan, not react. Retraining money for farm workers, a register of who's going to be affected, and supermarkets paying into a fund. I'd probably stand for something in the union if they asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years suits someone like me. I'm not first, I'm second, and five years is enough for the first lot to make the mistakes. I'd probably end up running the machines, or the people who run the machines, for a couple of years before it all goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one or two I'd do a proper course on farm automation once the college had one, not a weekend thing. I'd keep saving and pay the flat down so I own it outright before 2031. I'd also take a union role and set up a scheme with two other farms to retrain pickers as machine operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a useful way. Like the week before a big harvest when you know it's coming and you can plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd end up running the machines for a couple of years before it all goes. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd hope I'm useful somewhere else, maybe helping run a co-op or a local food scheme. I genuinely don't know past 2031. Nobody does, and I'd rather say that than pretend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want supermarkets paying into a fund. Do you think they would?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not unless they're made to. They'd say it's the government's job. That's why I'd want a law, not a promise.

S3.say: She'd say this is the moment for the union and the government to plan instead of react: retraining money for farm workers, a register of who will be affected and supermarkets paying into a fund. She'd stand for a union role if asked.
S3.think: She privately thinks five years suits her: she's never first, and five years lets the early adopters make the mistakes. She expects to run the machines, or the people who run them, for a few years before that work goes too.
S3.do: Takes a proper farm automation course in the first two years and pays off her flat before 2031. Takes on a union role and sets up a scheme with two other farms to retrain pickers as machine operators.
S3.feel: Anxious in a useful way, like the week before a big harvest when there's time to plan.
S3.quote: I'm not first, I'm second, and five years is enough for the first lot to make the mistakes.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is the timeline that fits Lena's steady style, and she says so plainly. She mixes self-interest (training, paying off the flat) with collective plans for the pickers. She is honest that she can't see beyond 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole career change, easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got no excuse this time. Ten years is enough to retrain every picker and supervisor in the country if anyone bothers. I'd keep saying it at union meetings until people were sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, with ten years I'd move out of farming on purpose, not because I'm pushed. I'd probably go into something like food policy or running a growers' co-op, the bit where people still decide things together. I like the field, but I'd rather choose to leave than be the last one standing in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give it two or three years of watching the machines get better, then go part-time at Brook Lane and do a part-time degree, maybe in food systems or something like that. I'd keep the flat paid down. I'd want to have helped set up the retraining scheme before I left, so I'm not walking out on the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly OK. There's even something exciting in having that much time to choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather choose to leave than be the last one standing. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum was a nurse on a ward they closed, and she stayed to the very end. She was so tired afterwards. I don't want to be the person turning off the lights in the cold store.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first step you'd take this year if you knew this was the picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask the college in town what they're planning, and look at part-time courses. And honestly, start using the AI tools properly, not just for translating, so I understand what's coming.

S4.say: She'd say ten years leaves no excuse: it's enough to retrain every picker and supervisor if anyone bothers. She'd keep raising it at union meetings until people were sick of hearing it.
S4.think: With ten years she'd leave farming by choice, likely for food policy or running a growers' co-op. She'd rather choose to go than be the last one left in the field.
S4.do: Watches the machines improve for two or three years, then goes part-time at the farm and starts a part-time degree in food systems. Helps set up the pickers' retraining scheme before she leaves and starts using AI tools properly this year.
S4.feel: Mostly OK with some unease, and even a little excited by having time to choose.
S4.quote: I don't want to be the person turning off the lights in the cold store.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Lena plans a deliberate exit rather than a defence, shaped by watching her mother stay too long on a closing ward. The extra time makes her more willing to use AI tools now. Her loyalty to the crew still sets the order of her plans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not even for me, for the crew. What would help is income support that reaches seasonal workers too, not only people with local contracts, and making supermarkets pay into it rather than pocketing the savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about food. If robots grow everything, who decides what gets grown and who gets it? I think about that more than about my own job, honestly.

headlineQuote: I've got savings and a flat, so I'm not on the street, but I wouldn't know what I'm for.
portrait: Lena Quinn is a 27-year-old field supervisor on a large vegetable farm that grows for supermarkets, running a summer crew of about forty pickers. She uses AI now and then and adopts new things once a neighbour has proven them. In every picture she thinks of her crew first and blames supermarket buyers for most of what's wrong in farming. The fast AGI picture leaves her safe but lost; five years suits her steady pace; ten years lets her plan a deliberate move into food policy or co-op work. Her cushion protects her, and she feels it puts a duty on her to help others.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, mainly for her seasonal crew, who have the least savings and the fewest protections.
whatWouldHelp: Income support that reaches seasonal workers as well as locals, paid for partly by supermarkets instead of them keeping the savings.
